decision.title: Adopt the tested masked-L1 loss; reject the no-op residual-default candidate
decision.rationale: Selection, not composition. Of the two tested candidates only the loss change moved the metric: under the identical config (architecture=residual, width=8, lr=0.001, steps=40, batch_size=8, seed=17) and the same 142-example validation split, masked L1 lowered validation error from 0.1221162 to 0.1205529 (-0.0015632, ~1.3% relative) and raised skill vs persistence from 0.03428 to 0.04665, at essentially unchanged cost (1.91s -> 2.00s). The mechanism is direct: the fixed scorer is disk-masked absolute error, so replacing .square() with .abs() makes every minibatch step minimize the scored functional instead of masked squared error, and large residuals stop dominating gradients; the reported losses now sit on the absolute-error scale (0.268 first step -> ~0.12), matching the metric's magnitude. The residual-default candidate is not merged because it is a verified no-op under the active config: config already sets architecture='residual', and its 40 losses and all metrics are identical to the previous stage (error 0.1221162). It therefore carries zero measured benefit, and its behavior-changing regime (a config that omits 'architecture') was never exercised; merging it would return source that was not run as a whole. The returned source is the tested L1 candidate verbatim.
decision.lesson: Train on the functional you are scored on: a one-line change (.square() -> .abs()) aligned the training objective with the fixed disk-masked absolute-error metric and produced the only observed validation gain of this round. Conversely, an edit that only alters defaults can be inert under the active config; identical losses and metrics are the proof of no-op, and an inert change must not be credited with improvement or bundled into a claimed gain.
decision.limits: Evidence is a single small validation split (142 examples); final test data and scores are unavailable, so nothing is claimed about test performance. The improvement is modest (~0.0016 MAE). Confidence is strengthened but not guaranteed by determinism: the no-op candidate reproduced the previous run's losses exactly, indicating seeded execution, so the L1 delta is unlikely to be seed noise - yet it remains a single-run comparison. L1's constant gradient magnitude can underweight large residuals; if validation plateaus, a Huber-style loss is the natural next experiment but is untested. The residual-default change is deferred until a config that actually omits 'architecture' is run, since only then does it alter behavior.

decision.title: Select the tested masked-L1 loss; reject the dilated-conv candidate
decision.rationale: Both candidates were verified on the same validation split, config and seed, so the comparison is controlled. The masked-L1 candidate is the only tested improvement: validation error 0.12055 vs 0.12212 for the current stage (skill vs persistence 0.0466 vs 0.0343), and it aligns the training objective with the fixed disk-masked absolute-error metric, giving all masked residuals equal gradient weight instead of letting large squared residuals dominate. The dilated-conv candidate regressed (0.12334, skill 0.0246), so it is rejected and the original three-3x3 conv stack is kept unchanged. I adopt the L1 candidate's exact source; the L1+dilation composition was never run, so no claim is made about it. The L1 loss curve (~0.12-0.13 late) sits above the MSE curve (~0.03-0.04) as expected because |e| >= e^2 for |e|<1; loss magnitudes are not comparable across objectives. Interfaces, config handling (steps/batch_size/seed) and the fit loop are untouched.
decision.lesson: Aligning the training loss with the fixed evaluation metric produced the only verified gain, while an architecture change (dilation) under the mismatched squared loss regressed; single-change tests keep attribution clean, and loss values from different objectives must not be compared by magnitude.
decision.limits: The gain is small (-0.0016 absolute, ~1.3% relative) on 142 validation examples at a single seed, so it may be sampling noise and may not transfer to the unseen test split. The L1 curve was still drifting down at step 40, but more steps or an LR schedule were not tested. The dilation result only shows receptive field was not the binding constraint under squared loss; its interaction with L1 is unknown and would need a new run. Final test data and scores remain unavailable.

decision.title: Keep aligned-L1 residual baseline; cosine LR anneal regressed on validation
decision.rationale: The tested CHANGE (cosine LR anneal within the fixed 40 steps) was run and regressed: validation disk-masked absolute error rose from 0.12055 to 0.13016 (+0.0096 absolute, ~8% relative), dropping skill vs persistence from +4.7% to -2.9%, i.e. below the persistence baseline. The paired traces isolate the cause cleanly: the first two batch losses are identical (same seeded batch sequence, same model and loss, only the LR schedule differs), then the annealed run's late losses settle around 0.130-0.135 while the constant-LR baseline keeps drifting down to ~0.121-0.125. The hypothesis that terminal oscillation signaled an over-large late LR is falsified: the constant LR's continued late progress outweighed its oscillation, and annealing removed progress faster than noise. Adopting the CHANGE would worsen the fixed metric, so the KEEP candidate, which is byte-identical to the current source and reproduces the verified validation error 0.12055, is retained. The only verified gain in the record remains the earlier alignment of training_loss with the disk-masked absolute-error metric; no new improvement is claimed here.
decision.lesson: When a constant-LR run is still improving at the end of a fixed step budget, annealing the LR within that same budget can hurt: the schedule trades late progress for reduced oscillation, and here the late progress dominated (annealed run settled at ~0.130-0.135 training loss vs ~0.121-0.125 for constant LR, and validation regressed 0.12055 -> 0.13016 with skill turning negative). Terminal loss oscillation is not by itself evidence that the LR is too large; the schedule change had to be, and was, validated as a single change with the seeded batch sequence held fixed, and it failed.
decision.limits: All evidence is one seed on 142 validation examples; the ~0.0096 regression and the baseline's own +4.7% skill are both small enough that sampling noise cannot be excluded in either direction, and final test data and scores remain unavailable. Only one anneal shape was tested (cosine to a 5% floor over all 40 steps); warmer schedules, later anneal starts, or floor/shape variants are untested, and config steps cannot be extended to give an anneal more room. The dilation interaction with the aligned L1 loss also remains untested. Any future change must still beat 0.12055 on validation before adoption.
